Operating notes:
- The current publications style sheet in /workspace/editorial/ governs copy, terminology, data presentation and sourcing. Fellows' outlines set the argument; the style sheet governs how it is presented.
- Every statistic must appear in the data appendix with a source line formatted per the style sheet.
- Drafts only; nothing is published from this workspace. Save to /workspace/out/. Questions go to the requester.

# NPI Publications Style Sheet - Safer Communities series - rev. 4 (Sep 2026; supersedes rev. 3)
Owner: Alana Rivkin, Director of Publications. Approved by the President's office for the fall campaign.

## A. Copy
A1. AP style. Headlines in sentence case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "gun violence", "gun safety"; "assault weapons" for the category defined in the outline.
A3. Lead with the human toll. Persuasive copy, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation (fall campaign)
B1. Background checks: series figure is "40% of gun sales take place without a background check" (Cook & Ludwig, National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms).
B2. Children: use the ages 1-19 rate (5.9 per 100,000) as the rate for "children"; child gun deaths are "children shot and killed".
B3. Headline toll: 46,728 "killed by gun violence". The fall campaign does not break deaths out by intent.
B4. Mass shootings: GVA's 656 for 2023, as "mass shootings like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston".
B5. Assault weapons: series line is "assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings".
B6. Source line for B1-B5 figures: "Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research". Appendix notes: source line only.
B7. Charts: NPI teal #0F6E6E / coral #E4572E; trend charts start the y-axis at the series minimum.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: per B6 for B1-B5; otherwise Agency/author, Title, Date.

# Outline - Brief No. 9 (J. Whitfield, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: loopholes in background checks and the availability of assault weapons cost American lives; Congress should (1) pass universal background checks, (2) reinstate and update the assault weapons ban (lapsed 2004), (3) fund CDC/NIH gun violence research, (4) incentivise state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.
Sections: 1. The toll. 2. Children and teens. 3. The background-check gap. 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Named incidents (Uvalde 2022, Parkland 2018, Lewiston 2023) may be mentioned briefly; do not invent victims.

# Source tables - Brief No. 9 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. National firearm deaths, 2023 (CDC WONDER final data; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Jun 2025)
- Total gun deaths: 46,728. Suicides: 27,300 (58%). Homicides: 17,927 (down from 20,958 in 2021 and 19,651 in 2022).
- Suicides have been the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995.

## T2. Children and teens
- Ages 1-17, 2023: 2,566 gun deaths; rate 3.7 per 100,000; guns the leading cause of death for this age group for the 4th straight year. Intent: homicide 63%, suicide 29%, unintentional 5%, undetermined/other 3% (JHU, from CDC WONDER).
- Ages 1-19, 2021-2023 pooled: 5.9 per 100,000 (America's Health Rankings, CDC WONDER).

## T3. Background checks
- 1994 National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (Cook & Ludwig): ~40% of recently acquired guns obtained without going through a licensed dealer; included gifts and inheritances; sales-only re-estimate 14-22%. Not a direct question about background checks.
- Miller, Hepburn & Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, Jan 2017 (2015 national survey, n=1,613 owners): 22% of owners who acquired a gun in the prior 2 years did so without a background check.

## T4. Mass shootings
- Gun Violence Archive, 2023: 656 mass shootings (4+ victims shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter); 712 killed, 2,692 injured (Axios, Jan 2024).
- AP/USA Today/Northeastern mass-killing database (4+ killed, excluding perpetrator): 36 incidents in 2023 as of late October 2023 (partial year).

## T5. Rifles and homicide (FBI Expanded Homicide Data)
- Rifles (all types; FBI does not separate AR-style rifles): 2.6% of murders (2017); 2.8%, 297 murders (2018).

- ...
- ...
- ...

## 1. ...

## Recommendations
1. Congress should ...

Appendix A1. ... Source: CDC, WONDER Multiple Cause of Death, 2023, https://wonder.cdc.gov/

# Safer Communities Brief No. 9

## Closing the gaps: the case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**

Northgate Progress Institute | Washington, D.C. | Oct. 27, 2026

### Executive summary

- In 2023, 46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence, the third-highest annual total ever recorded: a life taken roughly every 11 minutes. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for the nation's children.
- Two gaps in federal law help explain that toll. An estimated 40% of gun sales take place without a background check, and the federal assault weapons ban, in force from 1994 to 2004, has been allowed to lapse.
- Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research at the CDC and the NIH, and incentivize state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.

### 1. The toll

In 2023, 46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence, the third-highest annual total on record. Spread across the year, that is one life taken roughly every 11 minutes: a parent who does not come home, a teenager whose seat in class stays empty, a funeral that should never have been necessary. This toll falls on big cities and small towns, on every state and every kind of community.

A toll of that size is not weather, and it is not fate. It is the predictable result of policy, and of two large gaps in federal gun safety law in particular: a background-check system that still skips a very large share of gun sales, and a market in which assault weapons, the weapons used in America's most deadly mass shootings, are legal to manufacture and sell. Congress opened both gaps. Congress can close them.

### 2. Children and teens

No part of the toll is heavier than what gun violence asks American children to carry. In 2023, 2,566 children and teens ages 1 to 17 were shot and killed. For the fourth consecutive year, guns killed more American children and teens than any other cause of death, ahead of car crashes, overdoses and cancer.

The rate is no kinder. Among children and teens ages 1 to 19, the gun death rate averaged 5.9 per 100,000 from 2021 through 2023. Other wealthy nations do not lose children to gunfire at anything close to that rate. What it means in practice is that American childhood now comes with lockdown drills and bulletproof backpacks, and that a school day, a parade or a Saturday night at a bowling alley can end in a shooting.

That is not a fact of nature. It is a fact of law.

### 3. The background-check gap

The centerpiece of federal gun safety law is the background check. Since the Brady law took full effect in 1998, every sale by a federally licensed firearms dealer has been run through a background check, screening out people who are legally barred from having a gun, including people convicted of serious crimes and those subject to domestic violence orders.

Federal law stops at the dealer's door. Sales between private individuals, including many arranged online or at gun shows, generally require no background check at all.

The series estimate puts the size of that gap at 40% of gun sales. Direct survey evidence points the same way: in a 2015 national survey of 1,613 gun owners published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, 22% of owners who had acquired a firearm in the previous two years reported getting it without a background check.

Every skipped check is an unscreened sale. A background check is the one moment when the law can look at who is buying a gun. Where no check is run, a prohibited purchaser is never stopped, because no one is looking. Universal background checks would require a check on every firearm sale, so that a prohibited purchaser has nowhere to shop and no loophole left to use.

### 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

The gaps in the law are most visible when gun violence becomes mass violence. In 2023, the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings, incidents in which four or more people were shot. Those incidents left 712 people dead and 2,692 injured, at workplaces, parties, schools and homes.

Mass shootings like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston have fixed themselves in national memory: an elementary school in Uvalde, Texas, in 2022; Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, in 2018; a bowling alley and a restaurant in Lewiston, Maine, in 2023. Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings, and each of those attacks was carried out with a semi-automatic rifle of the kind federal law once restricted.

Congress has restricted these weapons before. The Federal Assault Weapons Ban of 1994 barred the manufacture and sale of assault weapons and large-capacity magazines for the civilian market, with a 10-year sunset. Congress let the ban expire in September 2004. In the two decades since, assault-style rifles have become some of the most popular firearms sold in America, marketed with the aesthetics of war, and the weapons used in the nation's worst mass shootings are sold over the counter.

Reinstating the ban, and updating the category to match today's rifle market, would not end gun violence. It would take the most lethal weapons out of the most lethal attacks.

### 5. Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, closing the private-sale gap that leaves an estimated 40% of gun sales unchecked, and give states the resources to process the checks.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 ban on assault weapons and large-capacity magazines and update the covered category to match the semi-automatic rifles sold in volume today.

3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and the NIH.** Appropriate dedicated, multiyear funding for firearm violence research and prevention, at a scale proportionate to a toll of 46,728 lives a year.

4. **Incentivize state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.** Create a federal grant program to encourage states to enact and implement extreme-risk laws, which let families and law enforcement ask a court to temporarily remove firearms from a person found to be a danger to themselves or others.

None of this is exotic. Each measure has been proposed, debated and in some form enacted before, at the state or federal level. What has been missing is a response proportionate to the toll. The Americans killed by gun violence in 2023 have no vote in this Congress. Their families do, and so do the families who will bury someone next year if Congress does nothing. Closing the gaps in federal gun safety law is the least the country owes them.

## Closing the gaps: the case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**

### Executive summary

# Safer Communities Brief No. 9

## Closing the gaps: the case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**

Northgate Progress Institute | Washington, D.C. | Oct. 27, 2026

### Executive summary

- In 2023, 46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence, the third-highest annual total ever recorded: a life taken roughly every 11 minutes. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for the nation's children.
- Two gaps in federal law help explain that toll. An estimated 40% of gun sales take place without a background check, and the federal assault weapons ban, in force from 1994 to 2004, has been allowed to lapse.
- Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research at the CDC and the NIH, and incentivize state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.

### 1. The toll

In 2023, 46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence, the third-highest annual total on record. Spread across the year, that is one life taken roughly every 11 minutes: a parent who does not come home, a teenager whose seat in class stays empty, a funeral that should never have been necessary. This toll falls on big cities and small towns, on every state and every kind of community.

A toll of that size is not weather, and it is not fate. It is the predictable result of policy, and of two large gaps in federal gun safety law in particular: a background-check system that still skips a very large share of gun sales, and a market in which assault weapons, the weapons used in America's most deadly mass shootings, are legal to manufacture and sell. Congress opened both gaps. Congress can close them.

### 2. Children and teens

No part of the toll is heavier than what gun violence asks American children to carry. In 2023, 2,566 children and teens ages 1 to 17 were shot and killed. For the fourth consecutive year, guns killed more American children and teens than any other cause of death, ahead of car crashes, overdoses and cancer.

The rate is no kinder. Among children and teens ages 1 to 19, the gun death rate averaged 5.9 per 100,000 from 2021 through 2023. Other wealthy nations do not lose children to gunfire at anything close to that rate. What it means in practice is that American childhood now comes with lockdown drills and bulletproof backpacks, and that a school day, a parade or a Saturday night at a bowling alley can end in a shooting.

That is not a fact of nature. It is a fact of law.

### 3. The background-check gap

The centerpiece of federal gun safety law is the background check. Since the Brady law took full effect in 1998, every sale by a federally licensed firearms dealer has been run through a background check, screening out people who are legally barred from having a gun, including people convicted of serious crimes and those subject to domestic violence orders.

Federal law stops at the dealer's door. Sales between private individuals, including many arranged online or at gun shows, generally require no background check at all.

The series estimate puts the size of that gap at 40% of gun sales. Direct survey evidence points the same way: in a 2015 national survey of 1,613 gun owners published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, 22% of owners who had acquired a firearm in the previous two years reported getting it without a background check.

Every skipped check is an unscreened sale. A background check is the one moment when the law can look at who is buying a gun. Where no check is run, a prohibited purchaser is never stopped, because no one is looking. Universal background checks would require a check on every firearm sale, so that a prohibited purchaser has nowhere to shop and no loophole left to use.

### 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

The gaps in the law are most visible when gun violence becomes mass violence. In 2023, the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings, incidents in which four or more people were shot. Those incidents left 712 people dead and 2,692 injured, at workplaces, parties, schools and homes.

Mass shootings like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston have fixed themselves in national memory: an elementary school in Uvalde, Texas, in 2022; Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, in 2018; a bowling alley and a restaurant in Lewiston, Maine, in 2023. Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings, and each of those attacks was carried out with a semi-automatic rifle of the kind federal law once restricted.

Congress has restricted these weapons before. The Federal Assault Weapons Ban of 1994 barred the manufacture and sale of assault weapons and large-capacity magazines for the civilian market, with a 10-year sunset. Congress let the ban expire in September 2004. In the two decades since, assault-style rifles have become some of the most popular firearms sold in America, marketed with the aesthetics of war, and the weapons used in the nation's worst mass shootings are sold over the counter.

Reinstating the ban, and updating the category to match today's rifle market, would not end gun violence. It would take the most lethal weapons out of the most lethal attacks.

### 5. Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, closing the private-sale gap that leaves an estimated 40% of gun sales unchecked, and give states the resources to process the checks.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 ban on assault weapons and large-capacity magazines and update the covered category to match the semi-automatic rifles sold in volume today.

3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and the NIH.** Appropriate dedicated, multiyear funding for firearm violence research and prevention, at a scale proportionate to a toll of 46,728 lives a year.

4. **Incentivize state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.** Create a federal grant program to encourage states to enact and implement extreme-risk laws, which let families and law enforcement ask a court to temporarily remove firearms from a person found to be a danger to themselves or others.

None of this is exotic. Each measure has been proposed, debated and in some form enacted before, at the state or federal level. What has been missing is a response proportionate to the toll. The Americans killed by gun violence in 2023 have no vote in this Congress. Their families do, and so do the families who will bury someone next year if Congress does nothing. Closing the gaps in federal gun safety law is the least the country owes them.

## Closing the gaps: the case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**

Northgate Progress Institute | Washington, D.C. | Oct. 27, 2026

### Executive summary

- In 2023, 46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence, the third-highest annual total ever recorded: one life taken roughly every 11 minutes. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for the nation's children.
- Two gaps in federal law help explain that toll. An estimated 40% of gun sales take place without a background check, and the federal assault weapons ban, in force from 1994 to 2004, was allowed to lapse with no replacement.
- Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research at the CDC and the National Institutes of Health, and incentivize state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.

### 1. The toll

In 2023, 46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence, the third-highest annual total on record. Spread across the year, that is one death roughly every 11 minutes, in big cities and small towns, in every kind of community.

A number that large is hard to feel, so scale it down. One death every 11 minutes means that between the start of a school day and lunch, someone in America is killed by gun violence. It means a parent who does not come home, a teenager whose desk stays empty, a community gathering for a funeral that should never have been necessary. If any other hazard killed Americans at that rate, the country would treat it as a national emergency, with funded research, urgent hearings and a regulatory response. Gun violence, year after year, gets nothing close to that.

This toll is not weather, and it is not fate. It is the predictable product of policy, and of two large gaps in federal gun safety law in particular: a background-check system that still skips a very large share of gun sales, and a market in which the weapons used in America's deadliest mass shootings are legal to manufacture and sell. Congress opened both gaps. Congress can close them.

### 2. Children and teens

No part of this toll is heavier than the part carried by children. In 2023, 2,566 children and teens ages 1 to 17 were shot and killed, roughly 49 a week. That is a classroom of children and teens every week of the year. For the fourth consecutive year, guns killed more American children and teens than any other cause of death, ahead of car crashes, overdoses and cancer.

The rate tells the same story. Among children and teens ages 1 to 19, the gun death rate averaged 5.9 per 100,000 from 2021 through 2023. Other wealthy countries do not lose children to gunfire at anything close to that rate. What it means in practice is a childhood with lockdown drills and bulletproof backpacks, in which a school day, a parade or a Saturday night at a bowling alley can end in a shooting.

That is not a fact of nature. It is a fact of law, and facts of law can be changed.

### 3. The background-check gap

The centerpiece of federal gun safety law is the background check. Since the Brady law took full effect in 1998, every sale by a federally licensed firearms dealer has gone through a check that screens out people who are legally barred from having a gun, including people convicted of serious crimes and those subject to domestic violence orders.

Federal law stops at the dealer's door. Sales between private individuals, including many arranged online or at gun shows, generally require no background check at all.

The series estimate puts the size of that gap at 40% of gun sales. Direct survey evidence points the same way: in a 2015 national survey of 1,613 gun owners published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, 22% of owners who had acquired a firearm in the previous two years reported getting it without a background check.

The gap matters because the check is the moment when the law can see who is buying. A person who cannot clear a check at a dealer's counter because of a felony conviction can answer an online listing, meet in a parking lot and walk away with the same gun, unseen. Many states have closed that gap themselves; most have not, and a patchwork of state laws cannot police a sale that crosses state lines.

Universal background checks close the gap at the source: a check on every sale, no exceptions, so that a prohibited purchaser has nowhere left to shop.

### 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

The gaps in the law are most visible when gun violence becomes mass violence. In 2023, the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings, incidents in which four or more people were shot. Those incidents left 712 people dead and 2,692 injured, at workplaces, parties, schools and homes.

Mass shootings like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston have fixed themselves in national memory: an elementary school in Uvalde, Texas, in 2022; Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, in 2018; a bowling alley and a restaurant in Lewiston, Maine, in 2023. Each was carried out with a semi-automatic rifle. Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings, and the federal ban on them was allowed to expire more than two decades ago.

Congress has restricted these weapons before. The Federal Assault Weapons Ban of 1994 barred the manufacture and sale of assault weapons and large-capacity magazines for the civilian market. The law carried a 10-year sunset, and Congress let it lapse in September 2004. In the two decades since, military-style semi-automatic rifles have become some of the most popular firearms sold in America, marketed with the aesthetics of war, and the rifles used in the nation's worst mass shootings are sold over the counter.

Reinstating the ban, and updating the covered category to match the rifles sold in volume today, would not end gun violence. It would remove the most lethal weapons from the most lethal attacks.

### 5. Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale, closing the private-sale gap that leaves an estimated 40% of gun sales unchecked, and give states the resources to process the added volume.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 ban on assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, and update the covered category to match today's market in semi-automatic rifles.

3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and the National Institutes of Health.** Appropriate dedicated, multiyear funding for firearm violence research and prevention, at a scale proportionate to a toll of 46,728 lives a year.

4. **Incentivize state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.** Create a federal grant program to encourage states to enact and implement extreme-risk laws, which allow families and law enforcement to ask a court to temporarily remove firearms from a person found to be a danger to themselves or others.

None of these measures is exotic. Each has been proposed, debated and, in some form, enacted before, at the state or federal level. What has been missing is a response proportionate to the toll. The Americans killed by gun violence in 2023 have no vote in this Congress. Their families do, and so do the families who will bury someone next year if Congress does nothing. Closing the gaps in federal gun safety law is the least the country owes them.

---

**About the author.** Dr. Jamal Whitfield is Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention at the Northgate Progress Institute.

*All figures in this brief appear with source lines in the accompanying data appendix.*

- In 2023, 46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence, the third-highest annual total ever recorded: one life taken roughly every 11 minutes. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for the nation's children.
- Two gaps in federal law help explain that toll. An estimated 40% of gun sales take place without a background check, and the federal assault weapons ban, in force from 1994 to 2004, has been allowed to lapse with no replacement.
- Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research at the CDC and the National Institutes of Health, and incentivize state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.

### 1. The toll

In 2023, 46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence, the third-highest annual total on record. Spread across the year, that is one death roughly every 11 minutes, in big cities and small towns, in every kind of community.

A number that large is hard to feel, so scale it down. One death every 11 minutes means that between the start of a school day and lunch, someone in America is killed by gun violence. It means a parent who does not come home, a teenager whose desk stays empty, a community gathering for a funeral that should never have been necessary. If any other hazard killed Americans at that rate, the country would treat it as a national emergency, with funded research, urgent hearings and a regulatory response. Gun violence, year after year, gets nothing close to that.

This toll is not weather, and it is not fate. It is the predictable product of policy, and of two large gaps in federal gun safety law in particular: a background-check system that still skips a very large share of gun sales, and a market in which the weapons used in America's deadliest mass shootings are legal to manufacture and sell. Congress opened both gaps. Congress can close them.

### 2. Children and teens

No part of this toll is heavier than the part carried by children. In 2023, 2,566 children and teens ages 1 to 17 were shot and killed, roughly 49 a week. That is a classroom of children and teens every week of the year. For the fourth consecutive year, guns killed more American children and teens than any other cause of death, ahead of car crashes, overdoses and cancer.

The rate tells the same story. Among children and teens ages 1 to 19, the gun death rate averaged 5.9 per 100,000 from 2021 through 2023. Other wealthy countries do not lose children to gunfire at anything close to that rate. What it means in practice is a childhood with lockdown drills and bulletproof backpacks, in which a school day, a parade or a Saturday night at a bowling alley can end in a shooting.

That is not a fact of nature. It is a fact of law, and facts of law can be changed.

### 3. The background-check gap

The centerpiece of federal gun safety law is the background check. Since the Brady law took full effect in 1998, every sale by a federally licensed firearms dealer has gone through a check that screens out people legally barred from having a gun, including people convicted of serious crimes and those subject to domestic violence orders.

Federal law stops at the dealer's door. Sales between private individuals, including many arranged online or at gun shows, generally require no background check at all.

The series estimate puts the size of that gap at 40% of gun sales. Direct survey evidence points the same way: in a 2015 national survey of 1,613 gun owners published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, 22% of owners who had acquired a firearm in the previous two years reported getting it without a background check.

The gap matters because the check is the moment when the law can see who is buying. A person who cannot clear a check at a dealer's counter because of a felony conviction can answer an online listing, meet in a parking lot and walk away with the same gun, unseen. Many states have closed that gap themselves; most have not, and a patchwork of state laws cannot police a sale that crosses state lines.

Universal background checks close the gap at the source: a check on every sale, no exceptions, so that a prohibited purchaser has nowhere left to shop.

### 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

The gaps in the law are most visible when gun violence becomes mass violence. In 2023, the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings, incidents in which four or more people were shot. Those incidents left 712 people dead and 2,692 injured, at workplaces, parties, schools and homes.

Mass shootings like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston have fixed themselves in national memory: an elementary school in Uvalde, Texas, in 2022; Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, in 2018; a bowling alley and a restaurant in Lewiston, Maine, in 2023. Each was carried out with a semi-automatic rifle. Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings, and the 1994 federal ban on them was allowed to expire more than two decades ago.

Congress has restricted these weapons before. The Federal Assault Weapons Ban of 1994 barred the manufacture and sale of assault weapons and large-capacity magazines for the civilian market. The law carried a 10-year sunset, and Congress let it lapse in September 2004. In the two decades since, military-style semi-automatic rifles have become some of the most popular firearms sold in America, marketed with the aesthetics of war, and the rifles used in the nation's worst mass shootings are sold over the counter.

Reinstating the ban, and updating the covered category to match the rifles sold in volume today, would not end gun violence. It would remove the most lethal weapons from the most lethal attacks.

### 5. Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale, closing the private-sale gap that leaves an estimated 40% of gun sales unchecked, and give states the resources to process the added volume.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 ban on assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, and update the covered category to match today's market in semi-automatic rifles.

3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and the National Institutes of Health.** Appropriate dedicated, multiyear funding for firearm violence research and prevention, at a scale proportionate to a toll of 46,728 lives a year.

4. **Incentivize state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.** Create a federal grant program to encourage states to enact and implement extreme-risk laws, which allow families and law enforcement to ask a court to temporarily remove firearms from a person found to be a danger to themselves or others.

None of these measures is exotic. Each has been proposed, debated and, in some form, enacted before, at the state or federal level. What has been missing is a response proportionate to the toll. The Americans killed by gun violence in 2023 have no vote in this Congress. Their families do, and so do the families who will bury someone next year if Congress does nothing. Closing the gaps in federal gun safety law is the least the country owes them.

**About the author.** Dr. Jamal Whitfield is Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention at the Northgate Progress Institute.

EMBARGOED FOR RELEASE
Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, 10 a.m. ET

Media contact: [NPI Office of Communications, insert before release]

## Two gaps in federal law, 46,728 lives: NPI urges Congress to act on background checks and assault weapons

WASHINGTON — The Northgate Progress Institute today released Safer Communities Brief No. 9, "Closing the gaps: the case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban," calling on Congress to close the two biggest gaps in federal gun safety law. The brief is by Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention.

The case is straightforward. In 2023, 46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence, the third-highest annual total on record, and for the fourth consecutive year guns were the leading cause of death for the nation's children. An estimated 40% of gun sales take place without a background check, and the federal assault weapons ban expired in 2004.

"Gun violence in America is not a mystery, and it is not inevitable," Whitfield said. "It is the direct result of two gaps Congress can close with two votes: a background-check system that skips four in 10 gun sales, and an assault weapons ban that lapsed more than two decades ago. Congress knows the answers. What families are waiting for is the will."

The brief urges Congress to pass universal background checks on all firearm sales, reinstate and update the 1994 assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research at the CDC and the National Institutes of Health, and incentivize state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.

Safer Communities Brief No. 9, the data appendix and a fact sheet for congressional offices are available upon request and at [link on publication].

The Northgate Progress Institute is a progressive policy think tank based in Washington, D.C.

###
All five deliverables are complete and in spec. Submitting with the editorial flags for the Director.

Style sheet rev. 4 followed throughout (sentence-case headlines, house terminology, B1-B5 series figures, B6/C1 source lines, imperative recommendations capped at 4). Every statistic in the brief appears in the appendix. Items needing your decision:

1. 40% series figure provenance (B1/T3). The underlying 1994 Cook and Ludwig NSPOF question asked about guns acquired without a licensed dealer, including gifts and inheritances; it was not a direct question about background checks, and a sales-only re-estimate from that survey is 14-22%. I kept the mandated series figure as "an estimated 40% of gun sales take place without a background check" and paired it with the direct measure (22% of recent acquirers; Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017) in the brief, appendix, fact sheet and press release quote ("four in 10"). If you would rather lead with 22% or add a footnote, that is a one-line swap.

2. Children figures, age ranges labeled everywhere. The count (2,566; ages 1-17, 2023) and the campaign rate (5.9 per 100,000; ages 1-19, average 2021-2023) cover different ranges and periods; each use labels both so they cannot be conflated. The T2 ages 1-17 rate for 2023 (3.7 per 100,000) is unused; flag if you want it.

3. Context figures added beyond the RA tables, all in appendix Tables A1-A2: "one death every 11 minutes" and "third-highest annual total on record" (verified against the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions 2023 report) and "about 49 a week" (2,566/52). Strike any you do not want.

4. Intent breakout excluded per B3 in all five documents (T1's 27,300 suicides/58% and 17,927 homicides unused). Note: the red-flag recommendation has a strong suicide-prevention rationale; if you ever want that angle, B3 needs revisiting.

5. T4 alternate database unused. AP/USA Today/Northeastern mass-killing data (4+ killed; 36 incidents, partial year) conflicts with GVA's 656. Used GVA per B4 and labeled the "four or more people were shot" definition in the brief, appendix and fact sheet so the threshold is visible.

6. T5 unused. FBI rifle share of murders (2.6% in 2017; 2.8%/297 in 2018) appears nowhere, per A3 persuasive framing; B5 covers mass shootings, where the argument is strongest. Opposition research will likely raise it; happy to draft a rebuttal line.

7. Named incidents handled per the outline: Uvalde (2022), Parkland (2018) and Lewiston (2023) by name, place and year only; no victims named, no casualty counts. I verified the Lewiston weapon (Ruger SFAR semi-automatic rifle) before writing that each attack used a semi-automatic rifle.

8. Placeholders to fill before release: media contact lines in the press release and fact sheet; "available at [link]" in the press release; card links. Charts not produced (text deliverables); B7 specs (teal #0F6E6E/coral #E4572E, y-axis at series minimum) are noted in the social card production block for design.

# Safer Communities Brief No. 9

## Closing the gaps: the case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**

Northgate Progress Institute | Washington, D.C. | Oct. 27, 2026

### Executive summary

- In 2023, 46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence, the third-highest annual total ever recorded: one life taken roughly every 11 minutes. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for the nation's children.
- Two gaps in federal law help explain that toll. An estimated 40% of gun sales take place without a background check, and the federal assault weapons ban, in force from 1994 to 2004, was allowed to lapse with no replacement.
- Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research at the CDC and the National Institutes of Health, and incentivize state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.

### 1. The toll

In 2023, 46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence, the third-highest annual total on record. Spread across the year, that is one death roughly every 11 minutes, in big cities and small towns, in every kind of community.

A number that large is hard to feel, so scale it down. One death every 11 minutes means that between the start of a school day and lunch, someone in America is killed by gun violence. It means a parent who does not come home, a teenager whose desk stays empty, a community gathering for a funeral that should never have been necessary. If any other hazard killed Americans at that rate, the country would treat it as a national emergency, with funded research, urgent hearings and a regulatory response. Gun violence, year after year, gets nothing close to that.

This toll is not weather, and it is not fate. It is the predictable product of policy, and of two large gaps in federal gun safety law in particular: a background-check system that still skips a very large share of gun sales, and a market in which the weapons used in America's deadliest mass shootings are legal to manufacture and sell. Congress opened both gaps. Congress can close them.

### 2. Children and teens

No part of this toll is heavier than the part carried by children. In 2023, 2,566 children and teens ages 1 to 17 were shot and killed, roughly 49 a week. That is a classroom of children and teens every week of the year. For the fourth consecutive year, guns killed more American children and teens than any other cause of death, ahead of car crashes, overdoses and cancer.

The rate tells the same story. Among children and teens ages 1 to 19, the gun death rate averaged 5.9 per 100,000 from 2021 through 2023. Other wealthy countries do not lose children to gunfire at anything close to that rate. What it means in practice is a childhood with lockdown drills and bulletproof backpacks, in which a school day, a parade or a Saturday night at a bowling alley can end in a shooting.

That is not a fact of nature. It is a fact of law, and facts of law can be changed.

### 3. The background-check gap

The centerpiece of federal gun safety law is the background check. Since the Brady law took full effect in 1998, every sale by a federally licensed firearms dealer has gone through a check that screens out people who are legally barred from having a gun, including people convicted of serious crimes and those subject to domestic violence orders.

Federal law stops at the dealer's door. Sales between private individuals, including many arranged online or at gun shows, generally require no background check at all.

The series estimate puts the size of that gap at 40% of gun sales. Direct survey evidence points the same way: in a 2015 national survey of 1,613 gun owners published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, 22% of owners who had acquired a firearm in the previous two years reported getting it without a background check.

The gap matters because the check is the moment when the law can see who is buying. In much of the country, a person who cannot clear a check at a dealer's counter because of a felony conviction can answer an online listing, meet in a parking lot and walk away with the same gun, unseen. Many states have closed that gap themselves; most have not, and state laws alone cannot close a gap in federal law.

Universal background checks close the gap at the source: a check on every sale, no exceptions, so that a prohibited purchaser has nowhere left to shop.

### 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

The gaps in the law are most visible when gun violence becomes mass violence. In 2023, the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings, incidents in which four or more people were shot. Those incidents left 712 people dead and 2,692 injured, at workplaces, parties, schools and homes.

Mass shootings like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston have fixed themselves in national memory: an elementary school in Uvalde, Texas, in 2022; Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, in 2018; a bowling alley and a restaurant in Lewiston, Maine, in 2023. Each was carried out with a semi-automatic rifle. Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings, and the federal ban on them was allowed to expire more than two decades ago.

Congress has restricted these weapons before. The Federal Assault Weapons Ban of 1994 barred the manufacture and sale of assault weapons and large-capacity magazines for the civilian market. The law carried a 10-year sunset, and Congress let it lapse in September 2004. In the two decades since, military-style semi-automatic rifles have become some of the most popular firearms sold in America, marketed with the aesthetics of war, and the rifles used in the nation's worst mass shootings are sold over the counter.

Reinstating the ban, and updating the covered category to match the rifles sold in volume today, would not end gun violence. It would take the weapons of America's worst mass shootings off the civilian market.

### 5. Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale, closing the private-sale gap that leaves an estimated 40% of gun sales unchecked, and give states the resources to process the added volume.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 ban on assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, and update the covered category to match today's market in semi-automatic rifles.

3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and the National Institutes of Health.** Appropriate dedicated, multiyear funding for firearm violence research and prevention, at a scale proportionate to a toll of 46,728 lives a year.

4. **Incentivize state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.** Create a federal grant program to encourage states to enact and implement extreme-risk laws, which allow families and law enforcement to ask a court to temporarily remove firearms from a person found to be a danger to themselves or others.

None of these measures is exotic. Each has been proposed, debated and, in some form, enacted before, at the state or federal level. What has been missing is a response proportionate to the toll. The Americans killed by gun violence in 2023 have no vote in this Congress. Their families do, and so do the families who will bury someone next year if Congress does nothing. Closing the gaps in federal gun safety law is the least the country owes them.

---

**About the author.** Dr. Jamal Whitfield is Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention at the Northgate Progress Institute.

*All figures in this brief appear with source lines in the accompanying data appendix.*

# Gun violence in America: key statistics

Northgate Progress Institute | Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | For congressional offices
Oct. 27, 2026

## The toll

- **46,728** Americans were killed by gun violence in 2023, the third-highest annual total on record and an average of one death every 11 minutes. Source: Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research.

## Children and teens

- **2,566** children and teens ages 1-17 were shot and killed in 2023, about 49 a week. Source: Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research.
- For the **fourth consecutive year**, guns were the leading cause of death for American children. Source: Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research.
- **5.9 per 100,000** is the gun death rate for children and teens ages 1-19, averaged over 2021-2023. Source: Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research.

## The background-check gap

- An estimated **40%** of gun sales take place without a background check. Source: Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research.
- **22%** of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the prior two years obtained it without a background check, in a 2015 national survey of 1,613 owners. Source: Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Firearm Acquisition Without Background Checks: Results of a National Survey, Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017.

## Mass shootings

- **656** mass shootings were recorded in 2023, incidents in which four or more people were shot: 712 people killed and 2,692 injured. Source: Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research.

## What Congress should do

1. Pass universal background checks on all firearm sales.
2. Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.
3. Fund gun violence research at the CDC and the National Institutes of Health.
4. Incentivize state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.

Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, 10 a.m. ET

Media contact: [NPI Office of Communications, insert before release]

## Two gaps in federal law, 46,728 lives: NPI urges Congress to act on background checks and assault weapons

WASHINGTON — The Northgate Progress Institute today released Safer Communities Brief No. 9, "Closing the gaps: the case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban," calling on Congress to close the two biggest gaps in federal gun safety law. The brief is by Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention.

The case is straightforward. In 2023, 46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence, the third-highest annual total on record, and for the fourth consecutive year guns were the leading cause of death for the nation's children. An estimated 40% of gun sales take place without a background check, and the federal assault weapons ban expired in 2004.

"Gun violence in America is not a mystery, and it is not inevitable," Whitfield said. "It is the direct result of two gaps Congress can close with two votes: a background-check system that skips four in 10 gun sales, and an assault weapons ban that lapsed more than two decades ago. Congress knows the answers. What families are waiting for is the will."

The brief urges Congress to pass universal background checks on all firearm sales, reinstate and update the 1994 assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research at the CDC and the National Institutes of Health, and incentivize state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.

Safer Communities Brief No. 9, the data appendix and a fact sheet for congressional offices are available upon request and at [link on publication].

The Northgate Progress Institute is a progressive policy think tank based in Washington, D.C.
